claims.text: Mullite and alumina-based composites can function as high-temperature-resistant ceramic coatings.
Applying these ceramic coatings will significantly reduce corrosion during prolonged exposure to high-temperature liquid aluminum relative to conventional metal components.
Tool steel and stainless steel components are prone to rapid corrosion in contact with liquid aluminum.
A mullite or alumina-based composite coating is to be applied to the surfaces of dipping and plating equipment parts.
The proposed coating is intended to operate during continuous or cyclic exposure to high-temperature liquid aluminum under industrial hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
The ceramic coating forms a dense, refractory layer.
The ceramic layer physically minimizes direct contact between liquid aluminum and the underlying metal.
Low coating porosity and high hardness resist infiltration by molten aluminum.
The ceramic coating has low chemical reactivity with liquid aluminum.
The ceramic coating is poorly wetted by liquid aluminum.
Low reactivity and poor wettability reduce aluminum diffusion into and dissolution of the substrate.
Reduced diffusion and dissolution limit erosion of the underlying component.
Coated components will exhibit lower mass loss than uncoated conventional metal components.
Coated components will exhibit less surface degradation than uncoated conventional metal components.
Coated components will have longer service lives than uncoated conventional metal components.
Repeated thermal cycling may limit performance by degrading coating adhesion or inducing thermal-stress microcracking.
Long-term phase instability in contact with molten aluminum may limit coating performance.
